trace.topic: Why Now Is the Biggest Change in SaaS Sales in 15+ Years
trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should argue that SaaS sales has structurally changed, not just slowed temporarily.
It should identify at least one concrete driver such as AI, buyer expectations, efficiency pressure, or changes in outbound/inbound behavior.
It should explain what founders must change in response.
rubric_must_haves: Names the change clearly and early.
Explains both the cause and the founder response.
Includes an example tied to modern GTM or sales execution.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that SaaS sales is in a structural transition, with founders needing a sharper value proposition, more efficiency, and often a different go-to-market motion than the old growth-at-all-costs era. The lesson is not to wait for the old playbook to return, but to adapt hiring, messaging, and sales process to the new environment.

trace.answer: Why Now Is the Biggest Change in SaaS Sales in 15+ Years If you’ve been doing B2B sales even just a little while — you know what the traditional org chart looked like just a few years ago: 🤷‍♂️ Sales Rep 👉 AE 👉 Manager 👉 VP of Sales 👀 CRO 📞 SDR 👈 Inbound 👨‍💻 RevOps And then something shifted. Fast. First came the explosion of SDR roles across every company. Then came “Rev Ops” which turned out to be just a fancy way of saying “data analyst” for the sales team. Next came an army of AEs who didn’t really sell anymore, they just closed deals assigned to them by their managers and VPs of Sales. But here’s what nobody was talking about until recently: the biggest change isn’t any of these things. It’s what happened to your traditional headcount per deal. You can see below some very interesting data on how much human contact there used to be per prospect vs today. Today, most folks I talk to want to close deals without ever speaking with a human. Or have an FDE / Solutions Engineer do the demo for free. Or buy from someone they never met. That sounds crazy if you’re selling products you built yourself, right? How could anyone trust buying from someone they’ve never spoken to? Well, maybe it makes sense when the product already exists off-the-shelf. Even so, I would bet 50% of prospects now buy without ever talking to a live rep. That

retrieval_hits.text:
So it does seem like some of the biggest changes to the human side of SaaS are now coming. I’ve talked with three CEOs at leading vendors in sales and post-sales at $200m+ in ARR the past few weeks and they’ve all reinforced these are some of the biggest changes in a generation. What we’ve seen in the first 15 years of SaaS:
Specialization in sales
. Segment reps, and have closers close. The rise of the SDR and productizing outbound and qualifying inbound with humans
. Outbound is nothing new, but the formal role of the SDR exploded in the past decade. The rise of customer success as a new, empowered function. Everyone has fully staffed CS over the past decade. We’ve all become NRR, GRR, and CSAT experts, and CS owned it all. Human support remained important, at least for paying customers
. Sometimes begrudgingly, but everyone has some level of human support, especially for larger customers. In fact, leaders from Intercom to Front to Gorgias to Zendesk exploded as this function, while not remotely new, became standardized. The reality is this is all now changing, for the first time. AI isn’t the only reason, the real drive is efficiency. But AI is the accelerant:
#1. There is a general sense among the leaders in sales software that we will end up with fewer, better SDRs, and that the majority of email and follow-up will be done with AI. Salesloft, Outreach, Gong and more radically changed the space. But we may be looking at far more radical change in the coming few years.
#2. Customer Success has in many cases morphed into part of the sales team.
